Publishable fields only. A support case number, an account ID or a resource ID

tier: documented (a vendor document says so; needs a source read in full)
verified   (observed by running something here; needs an observation)
hypothesis (reasoned from adjacent facts; the vendor has not said it)

Seeded empty on install. The first claim goes in when someone writes one; until

claims.claim: ARP/AI's documented response to detected abnormal activity does not include refusing or delaying a write. The response vocabulary is a warning, an automatic snapshot, administrator classification as false positive or potential attack, and resumed monitoring.
claims.subject: ONTAP Autonomous Ransomware Protection (ARP/AI), ONTAP 9.16.1 and later

sources.note: The whole response flow is warning, snapshot, classification, clear-suspect. No step refuses an operation.
The ARP versus ARP/AI comparison table lists snapshot creation as the automatic action. Blocking is not among the listed behaviours.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether ARP/AI ever refuses a write in active mode. The vendor documentation enumerates the response flow, and the remaining uncertainty is about observed behaviour on a specific build rather than about intent, so it is being answered by measurement here rather than by asking.

claims.note: Absence of a documented blocking step is not the same as a measured absence of blocking. The design here treats ARP as detection only, which is the conservative direction; the measurement plan exists to turn this into an observation.

claims.claim: A name-mapping deny entry does not block SMB access on a volume with NTFS security style. Access is decided by the Windows credentials, and a user whose mapping fails falls back to the CIFS server's default UNIX user.
claims.subject: ONTAP name-mapping (win-unix) on NTFS security style volumes

sources.note: States that access is granted or denied on the Windows credentials because the volume is NTFS security style, and that a failed mapping falls back to the default UNIX user.
Security styles determine which permission type ONTAP uses for access control.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether name-mapping deny can block SMB on NTFS security style volumes. The vendor KB answers it directly.

claims.note: A sibling repository's automated-response addendum states the opposite in a table whose justification is reasoned rather than observed. When the Q2 measurement runs, the volume security style is recorded so the two statements can be settled against a run instead of against each other.

claims.claim: ARP does not make signature-based malware determinations about individual files. Its detection inputs are file activity, data entropy and file extension types.
claims.subject: ONTAP Autonomous Ransomware Protection, all generations

sources.note: Detection method is given as file activity, data entropy and extension types for ARP, and an AI model analysing entropy and file behaviour for ARP/AI. Neither is a signature scanner, and the page positions ARP as an additional layer alongside FPolicy and snapshots.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether ARP performs per-file malware identification. The vendor documentation states the detection inputs.

claims.note: This is why the layered design keeps a scanner (Vscan/ICAP or an agent) alongside ARP rather than treating ARP as a replacement.

claims.claim: On ARP/AI, a request to set the volume anti-ransomware state to dry_run lands as enabled, and neither a warning nor an error is returned. The learning mode is not selectable.
claims.subject: ONTAP REST API PATCH /storage/volumes/{uuid} anti_ransomware.state, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1

sources.note: Documents that ARP/AI has no learning period, which is consistent with dry_run not being a reachable state. The silent substitution itself is not documented.
Sibling repository record of the observation, including the read-back showing enabled.

claims.observation: 2026-08-15, ap-northeast-1, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1. PATCH with anti_ransomware.state=dry_run returned 200; a subsequent GET of anti_ransomware.state returned enabled. Disabling the same volume left the state at disable_in_progress for more than 10 minutes on a 20 GiB empty volume.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the API should reject or warn on an unreachable state value. Behaviour is observed and reproducible; the design consequence is to read back after PATCH rather than to trust the request, which does not depend on the vendor's answer.

claims.note: The design consequence: a verification plan cannot use learning mode as a safety net, and a handler must not echo the requested state back to a caller.

claims.claim: ARP's operation-rate detection inputs (file create, rename, delete) do not fire on an absolute rate. They fire on a surge relative to the historically observed value for that volume, so a volume with no history has nothing for the surge to be measured against. Separately, the never-seen-before-file-extension threshold counts files created or renamed with one new extension, not the number of distinct new extensions.
claims.subject: ONTAP anti-ransomware volume attack-detection-parameters

sources.note: Each of based-on-file-create-rate, -rename-rate and -delete-rate is described as an attack when the per-timeslot count surges by the corresponding notify percentage compared to the historically observed value. The never-seen-before duration parameter states that the threshold is a number of files created or renamed with the new extension within the duration.

States the threshold as the number of files observed with a new file extension for create/rename operations, which is the clearer wording of the two pages. Neither page scopes the create/rename/delete parameters by protocol.

support_inquiry.topic: How the surge baseline is established on a volume with no operation history. The CLI reference states the comparison is against the historically observed value; whether a fresh volume therefore never fires is a question for measurement, not for the vendor.

claims.note: Corrects one reading and bounds another. Bulk rename or delete is not outside ARP's inputs, it is outside the threshold. On the never-seen-before input, an adjacent run (2026-09-07, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1, ARP/AI, NFSv3, freshly created volumes) did exceed the file-count condition -- 1,000 files on one new extension against a threshold of 5 -- and saw no detection within 30 minutes against a 48-hour duration parameter. Whether that run tested the input at all depends on whether "for this duration" means within the window or sustained across it, which the reference does not settle. The retest is designed to satisfy either reading rather than to pick one. A separate point found while checking this: the parameter table is the set of toggleable inputs, not the set of detection inputs. Both pages document two always-enabled paths independent of these parameters -- per-file high-entropy detection, and combined extension-and-entropy detection -- so a non-detection cannot be attributed to any one parameter's behaviour.

claims.claim: The set of file extensions ONTAP treats as popular, and therefore safe, when relaxing-popular-file-extensions is true is not published. A tester cannot confirm that a chosen extension is outside that set.
claims.subject: ONTAP anti-ransomware relaxing-popular-file-extensions

sources.note: Describes the parameter as treating a predetermined commonly used extension such as .mp3 as safe, and gives one example rather than the set. No enumeration appears on the page.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the popular-extension set can be enumerated. It only affects test design here -- a ransomware extension is very unlikely to be in it -- so the measurement records the parameter value and states the assumption rather than resting on the answer.

claims.note: Recorded so that a later run does not read 'the extension was not popular' as established. It is an assumption, and the ledger says so.

claims.claim: The Attack Detected By field cannot identify which detection input raised an attack, and the reference does not settle what the field returns. The parameter line enumerates file and block while the description immediately below gives file_analysis and encryption_percentage_analysis. Even on the description's reading, two values stand against five or more toggleable inputs plus two always-enabled paths, so the field distinguishes neither individual inputs nor toggleable from always-on.
claims.subject: ONTAP security anti-ransomware volume show, -attack-detected-by

sources.note: Gives two different value sets for the same field on one page: 'The possible values are file, block' followed by descriptions of file_analysis and encryption_percentage_analysis. The state field is inconsistent the same way -- the parameter enumeration carries seven values including paused, the prose below lists six and drops paused. Also gives the attack-probability value set.
Enumerates the toggleable inputs and the two always-enabled paths, which is the other half of the mismatch.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether a finer attribution of the detecting input is exposed anywhere. The measurement works around it by recording per-suspect reasons and the entropy-stat output instead, so the answer would refine the method rather than unblock it.

claims.note: Recorded because a measurement that reports 'detected by file_analysis' invites the reader to conclude which parameter fired. It does not support that, and the value itself may not be what the page's description says. Raised as a request from the Adoption Playbook side to attribute detections to always-on versus toggleable paths; this field cannot answer it. The handling is to record the observed value verbatim and to read the seven-value state enumeration rather than the six-value prose, so that paused is not dropped.

claims.claim: Tamperproof snapshots and FabricPool cannot be enabled on the same ONTAP volume; how this applies to FSx for ONTAP capacity pool tiering is not established.
claims.subject: ONTAP snapshot locking (tamperproof snapshots), ONTAP 9.12.1 and later

sources.note: Lists FabricPool under unsupported features: because FabricPool requires the ability to delete data, FabricPool and snapshot locks cannot be enabled on the same volume.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the FabricPool restriction applies to FSx for ONTAP capacity pool tiering. The documents here state it as an inference and mark it unverified; no design decision rests on the answer.

claims.note: The NetApp statement is about FabricPool on ONTAP. FSx for ONTAP documentation was not found to state how snapshot locking interacts with capacity pool tiering, so that part is not established.

claims.claim: Malware Protection for AWS Backup does not scan FSx for ONTAP recovery points. The feature availability table leaves the Malware Protection column blank for FSx for ONTAP, and the GuardDuty page names EBS snapshots, EC2 AMIs and S3 recovery points.
claims.subject: AWS Backup feature availability, Malware Protection for AWS Backup

sources.note: The FSx for ONTAP row has check marks for cross-Region, cross-account, Audit Manager, incremental, restore testing and logically air-gapped vault, and blanks for continuous backup, full management, cold storage, item-level restore, backup search, backup tiering, Malware Protection and access points.
Overview names EBS snapshots, EC2 AMIs and S3 recovery points as examples of what is scanned.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether Malware Protection for AWS Backup covers FSx for ONTAP recovery points. The feature availability table answers it for the current release; the design keeps recovery point checks on FlexClone plus a scan through S3 Access Points either way.

claims.note: Coverage tables change. Recheck the table before relying on this.

claims.claim: A backup of a resource without full AWS Backup management that is encrypted with an AWS managed key cannot be copied to a logically air-gapped vault. FSx for ONTAP lacks full management and defaults to an AWS managed key.
claims.subject: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault, resources without full AWS Backup management (FSx for ONTAP)

sources.note: Resources not supporting full management and encrypted with AWS managed keys cannot be copied to logically air-gapped vaults; the backup job completes in the standard vault with a 'Completed with issues - Unsupported encryption key' message. Amazon FSx is named among resources that go through a temporary recovery point.
Compatible encryption: for resource types that are not fully managed, the source must be encrypted with a customer managed key; AWS managed keys are not supported for them.
The AWS managed KMS key is the default key for FSx for ONTAP file systems and backups.
The Full management column is blank for FSx for ONTAP.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether an FSx for ONTAP file system on an AWS managed key can have its backups copied to a logically air-gapped vault. The developer guide states the constraint and the resulting job status.

claims.note: This is about the source file system's key. The vault's own encryption key is a separate choice (AWS owned key by default, or a customer managed key) and is covered by E-020.

claims.claim: FSx for ONTAP volume backups cover RW volumes only. DP, LSM, FlexCache and SnapMirror destination volumes, and SnapLock FlexGroup volumes, are not backed up, and a non-SnapLock backup cannot be restored as a SnapLock volume.
claims.subject: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume backups

sources.note: Backups support OntapVolumeType RW; DP, LSM and FlexCache or SnapMirror destination volumes are not supported. A SnapLock FlexGroup volume cannot be backed up. A SnapLock backup restores as SnapLock or non-SnapLock; a non-SnapLock backup cannot be restored as SnapLock.

support_inquiry.topic: Which FSx for ONTAP volume types can be backed up. The user guide lists them.

claims.note: A SnapMirror destination in a DR file system is therefore not a source for AWS Backup; back up the RW source volume instead.

claims.claim: Logically air-gapped vault sharing through AWS RAM targets individual account IDs, not organisations or OUs. A shared account can view and restore recovery points but cannot copy them.
claims.subject: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault sharing through AWS RAM

sources.note: A vault can be shared with individual AWS account IDs only, including accounts in another organisation, not with an organisation or OU. Shared accounts can view or restore a backup but not create a copy.

support_inquiry.topic: Sharing scope and rights for a shared logically air-gapped vault. The developer guide states both.

claims.note: The recovery account design depends on this: it restores, it does not hold its own copies.

claims.claim: Restore testing, recovery point indexing and malware scanning ignore temporary recovery points with a DELETE_AFTER_COPY lifecycle, which is the path FSx for ONTAP backups take into a logically air-gapped vault.
claims.subject: AWS Backup temporary recovery points (DELETE_AFTER_COPY) for logically air-gapped vaults

sources.note: Restore testing, indexing and scanning item: these ignore temporary recovery points with a DELETE_AFTER_COPY lifecycle. Amazon FSx is named among resources that cannot back up directly to the vault and go through a temporary recovery point, which is billed during its retention.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether restore testing can use the temporary recovery point. The developer guide states it does not; the design tests against recovery points in the vault instead.

claims.note: Restore testing still covers FSx for ONTAP; it is the temporary recovery point that is excluded.

claims.claim: A logically air-gapped vault's encryption key is set when the vault is created and cannot be changed afterwards, and Vault Lock compliance mode is always on for the vault.
claims.subject: AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault, encryption key and Vault Lock mode

sources.note: A KMS key can only be selected during vault creation and the vault cannot be changed or migrated to a different key. The comparison table says the vault is always locked with a vault lock in compliance mode.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the vault key or lock mode can be changed after creation. The developer guide states both are fixed.

claims.note: Both are irreversible decisions made at vault creation; the approval for them is routed to the Adoption Playbook.

claims.claim: Concurrent copy jobs into a logically air-gapped vault for Amazon FSx resources are limited to 5, and the quota is not adjustable (checked 2026-10-08).
claims.subject: AWS Backup quotas, concurrent copy jobs into a logically air-gapped vault for Amazon FSx

sources.note: Logically air-gapped vault quotas: the quotas are currently not adjustable; the FSx row gives 5 as the maximum number of concurrent copies.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the concurrent copy limit can be raised. The quotas page marks it as not adjustable; the design fits backup frequency to it.

claims.note: Quotas change; the figure carries its check date.

claims.claim: ARP is not relied on to detect read-only exfiltration. Its documented detection inputs are data entropy, file extension types and surges in file create, rename and delete rates; no documented detection condition fires on the volume of reads alone.
claims.subject: ONTAP Autonomous Ransomware Protection, all generations, read-only access

sources.note: Detection method: file activity, data entropy and file extension types (ARP); entropy and file behaviour (ARP/AI). The overview also says ARP processes data as it is written to or read from storage, so reads are seen; what is not documented is a detection condition driven by reads without encryption.

The toggleable inputs are create, rename and delete rate surges and never-seen-before extensions; the always-enabled paths are per-file high entropy and combined extension-and-entropy. None is a read-volume condition. Same reading as E-005.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether ARP raises an alert on bulk reads without encryption. The design already assumes it does not and routes exfiltration to audit logs and a SIEM, so an answer either way would not change the design.

claims.note: Phrased as 'not relied on' rather than 'does not detect'. If a read-driven detection exists, the documents here still hold, because they do not depend on ARP for exfiltration.

claims.claim: FSx for ONTAP controls act on file, object and block access and on management operations. SQL statements and API authorisation decisions made in the application or database layer are not observable from the storage layer.
claims.subject: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP data access protocols (SMB, NFS, S3 Access Points, iSCSI, NVMe/TCP)

sources.note: The SVM endpoints are NFS, SMB, iSCSI, NVMe over TCP and management; S3 access points are a further access path. These carry file, block and object operations.
Describes file systems, SVMs and volumes as the unit of storage and access.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the storage layer can see application-level queries. The boundary follows from what the protocols carry; confirming it would not change the design, which only routes readers to application-layer controls.

claims.note: When a database stores its files on an iSCSI or NVMe LUN, ONTAP sees blocks, not rows or statements (inference). A separate, compatible pattern exists: an application can run SQL queries against an external data source and store the query results as files or objects on FSx for ONTAP via S3 Access Points or NFS/SMB. In that pattern FSx for ONTAP sees the write of the result file, not the SQL statement or its authorisation decision; the claim is consistent with this use.

claims.claim: FPolicy receives NFS and SMB operations only; operations through an FSx for ONTAP S3 access point do not reach FPolicy.
claims.subject: ONTAP FPolicy with FSx for ONTAP S3 Access Points, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1

sources.note: Section 'FPolicy does not see this path at all': measured 2026-08-26 on ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1; an FPolicy event accepts only cifs, nfsv3 and nfsv4 as protocol and s3 is rejected.
The measurement record: no FPolicy notification for S3 access point data operations on UNIX and NTFS volumes, with file protocol controls on the same session that did notify.

claims.observation: 2026-08-26, ap-northeast-1, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1. S3 access point PUT, GET, DELETE and LIST raised no FPolicy notification on UNIX and NTFS volumes, while NFSv3 and SMB operations on the same volumes and FPolicy session did. The FPolicy event protocol accepted only cifs, nfsv3 and nfsv4.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether FPolicy can be made to see the S3 access point path. The accepted protocol values settle it for this build; the design covers the path with ARP for writes and with access point policy and IAM for the boundary.

claims.note: Recorded on one build (re-checked on 9.18.1P5 for the protocol enumeration in the Playbook note). Recheck on a later ONTAP release before relying on it.

claims.claim: The ONTAP native file access audit log records data operations through an FSx for ONTAP S3 access point (Source=HTTP or S3, with file name, operation, offset and byte count) but does not record the requesting principal.
claims.subject: ONTAP file access auditing through FSx for ONTAP S3 Access Points, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1

sources.note: Sections 2-1 to 2-4: S3 access point operations appear as audit events with Source HTTP (LIST with Source S3); SubjectUserName is Not Present and SubjectIP is an AWS-owned address that changes per call, so neither the IAM principal nor the source address can be recovered.

claims.observation: 2026-08-26, ap-northeast-1, ONTAP 9.18.1P3D1. With file_operations auditing enabled and an Everyone audit_success SACL applied, S3 access point data operations appeared as audit events with Source=HTTP, including file name, operation type, offset and bytes; no requester identity field was present.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether the audit log can carry the S3 requester. It is reproducible by observation, and the design does not expect the audit log to identify the requester on this path.

claims.note: The audit records require a SACL on the objects; enabling auditing alone records nothing.

claims.claim: For SMB object access events, ONTAP audits only the first read and the first write operation on an object, so the audit log does not count successive reads.
claims.subject: ONTAP SMB file access auditing (event 4663)

sources.note: Event 567/4663 note: ONTAP audits only the first SMB read and first SMB write operation (success or failure) on an object, to avoid excessive log entries when one client performs many successive operations.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether SMB auditing can record every read. The user guide states the behaviour; it only limits how the log is used to estimate volume.

claims.note: A caution about estimating read volume from the SMB audit log, not a design premise.

claims.claim: Amazon Macie analyses objects in S3 general purpose buckets that use one of six listed storage classes. Objects reached through FSx for ONTAP S3 Access Points use the FSX_ONTAP storage class and are outside that list.
claims.subject: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery, supported storage classes

sources.note: Macie analyses objects stored in an S3 general purpose bucket using a supported storage class: RRS, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Intelligent-Tiering, One Zone-IA, Standard and Standard-IA. Objects in other storage classes are skipped.
FSX_ONTAP is the only supported storage class for objects through an FSx for ONTAP access point.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether Macie can scan data through FSx for ONTAP S3 Access Points. The two pages together settle it for the current release; sensitive data detection here uses the companion repository's PII scanner.

claims.note: Corrects an earlier statement in the comparison document that Macie applies through S3 Access Points.

claims.claim: The CloudFormation resource types for FSx for ONTAP SVMs and volumes have no property that creates or enables an ONTAP file access auditing configuration; auditing is configured with the ONTAP CLI or REST API.
claims.subject: AWS::FSx::StorageVirtualMachine, AWS::FSx::Volume (OntapConfiguration)

sources.note: Properties are ActiveDirectoryConfiguration, FileSystemId, Name, RootVolumeSecurityStyle, SvmAdminPassword and Tags. None configures auditing.

Properties are AggregateConfiguration, CopyTagsToBackups, JunctionPath, OntapVolumeType, SecurityStyle, SizeInBytes, SizeInMegabytes, SnaplockConfiguration, SnapshotPolicy, StorageEfficiencyEnabled, StorageVirtualMachineId, TieringPolicy and VolumeStyle. None configures auditing.

Setting up auditing is a sequence of ONTAP commands: vserver audit create on the SVM, then vserver audit enable, then audit policies on files and folders. The page also requires sufficient free space in the volume that holds the converted logs and points to -rotate-limit for that.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether CloudFormation will expose ONTAP auditing. The manual step works regardless of the answer.

claims.note: Why the runbook carries a manual vserver audit create / enable step after the stack creates vol_audit_prod.

claims.claim: NetApp Console and NetApp System Manager are not supported for second-generation FSx for ONTAP file systems with more than one high-availability (HA) pair.
claims.subject: FSx for ONTAP management with NetApp applications (NetApp Console, NetApp System Manager)

sources.note: The page states 'NetApp Console isn't supported for second-generation file systems with more than one high-availability (HA) pair.' and, under using System Manager with NetApp Console, 'NetApp System Manager isn't supported for second-generation file systems with more than one HA pair.'

support_inquiry.topic: Whether NetApp Console / System Manager support second-generation file systems with more than one HA pair. The AWS user guide states they do not; this scopes which management plane is available on such configurations rather than driving a design decision.

claims.note: Used to scope the management-plane map: on second-generation file systems with more than one HA pair, the CLI and REST API are the available planes. Not a design premise; the map states reachability per plane.

claims.claim: Multi-admin verification is not supported on Cloud Volumes ONTAP; enabling it results in an unsupported configuration.
claims.subject: NetApp Cloud Volumes ONTAP, multi-admin verification (release notes for 9.15.1)

sources.note: The page, dated 12/04/2024, lists multi-admin verification under features not supported with Cloud Volumes ONTAP in all cloud providers and says enabling it results in an unsupported configuration. It is the 9.15.1 release notes; a later release may differ.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether a later Cloud Volumes ONTAP release supports multi-admin verification. The platform table in this document states the release the statement comes from, and no design rests on it.

claims.note: Version-bound. Recheck the current release notes before citing it for a later release.

claims.claim: Multi-admin verification could not be enabled or configured with the fsxadmin role on Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, ONTAP 9.18.1P6. The version has the feature (seven /security/multi-admin-verify endpoints), but fsxadmin is refused: the list of CLI commands the user can run (show-user-capability, read through the REST CLI pass-through; the CLI itself was not run over SSH) has no multi-admin-verify command, the fsxadmin role has no entry for it and its parent security is none, and the REST calls to enable it and to create an approval group returned HTTP 403. Observed on one file system, one version, as fsxadmin only.
claims.subject: ONTAP multi-admin verification on Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, fsxadmin role, ONTAP 9.18.1P6

sources.note: Describes security login role show-rest as listing the REST APIs of the version with their mapped CLI commands, whatever the user's privilege. Used to establish that the version has the multi-admin-verify endpoints.
The Adoption Playbook note lists availability of multi-admin verification on FSx for ONTAP as unconfirmed, before this observation.
A search for 'multi-admin' on the roles and users page returned no match, so the page neither lists nor excludes the feature. The AWS documentation read here says nothing either way.

claims.observation: 2026-11-04, ap-northeast-1, Single-AZ, ONTAP 9.18.1P6, as fsxadmin through the management endpoint. show-rest lists seven /security/multi-admin-verify endpoints. show-user-capability (1,744 commands, which matched the role-based calculation on 13 of 13 discriminating commands) lists none. The fsxadmin role has no multi-admin entry and its parent security is none with no query. PATCH /security/multi-admin-verify {enabled: true} returned 403 'not authorized for that command' once. POST /security/multi-admin-verify/approval-groups returned 403 once (an earlier call returned 400 because of a request body error). GET on the multi-admin-verify endpoints returned 403. Controls in the same session, GET /storage/snaplock/compliance-clocks and GET /security/roles, returned 200. SVM roles carry request entries (request: all; request approve and veto: none), and no cluster role carries a setup entry.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether another role or an AWS-side management route can configure multi-admin verification on FSx for ONTAP. fsxadmin is the delegated administrator and the design here does not rely on the feature, so an answer would add an option rather than unblock one.

claims.note: Observed once on one file system and one version, as fsxadmin. Other ONTAP versions, Multi-AZ, other roles and AWS-side routes were not checked. The multi-admin-verify command reference describes ONTAP in general and carries no run on fsxadmin; the documents here cite this entry wherever they list the feature. Data: docs/ontap-native/ontap-command-api-snapshot.md and docs/ontap-native/data/.

claims.claim: The AWS documentation read here lists, as inputs to AWS Security Agent and AWS Continuum, design documents, source code and running applications; it lists no storage-system configuration. The Adoption Playbook records that FSx for ONTAP management-plane settings are outside what it evaluates, as an unverified judgement.
claims.subject: AWS Security Agent (now part of AWS Continuum), evaluated targets

sources.note: Describes design review, threat modeling, code review and on-demand penetration testing of applications. Targets are design documents, source code and a target URL with authentication details. Storage configuration is not mentioned either way.
Continuum reasons over structured data that already exists in AWS (infrastructure, permissions, network topology, code); whether FSx for ONTAP settings are included is not stated.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether Continuum ingests FSx for ONTAP settings as context. No design here depends on it; the decision trees cover the storage side independently.

claims.note: Absence from a feature description is not a statement of absence. Treated as unknown, and the document says so.

claims.claim: AWS Security Agent on-demand penetration testing (now Continuum for Penetration Testing) reached general availability in March 2026 and added 6 regions in September 2026. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities reached general availability on 2026-10-22, in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Continuum for code scanning, threat modeling and design security review remain in preview; no GA announcement for them was found in What's New or the AWS blog as of 2026-11-04.
claims.subject: AWS Continuum / AWS Security Agent feature-level availability

sources.note: Announces GA of on-demand penetration testing.
Six additional regions for Continuum for Penetration Testing.
Announces GA of Continuum for code vulnerabilities on 2026-10-22; points to the AWS Region table for availability and does not name a region in the post itself.
Japanese translation of the same GA announcement.

support_inquiry.topic: Current availability per feature and region. Checked against What's New directly; availability changes, so re-check before adopting.

claims.note: Supersedes this document's earlier statement that Continuum for code vulnerabilities was in limited preview, which was accurate only as of the 2026-06-17 announcement. Corrected 2026-11-04. The specific regions for code vulnerabilities (US East N. Virginia, US West Oregon) were reported by a third party (dev.to) and a sibling repository's independent check, not read verbatim in the AWS post itself; treat the region list as needing a check against the AWS Region table before relying on it.

claims.claim: The REST path /security/anti-ransomware/volumes/{uuid} is not an endpoint of ONTAP 9.18.1P6 on FSx for ONTAP. The version's endpoint list has no such path, and a GET of /api/security/anti-ransomware/volumes returned HTTP 404.
claims.subject: ONTAP REST API, anti-ransomware volume path, ONTAP 9.18.1P6

claims.claim: A CloudWatch metric alarm is rejected when its alarm action names an SNS topic in a different Region. An alarm in us-west-2 cannot notify a topic in ap-northeast-1.
claims.subject: Amazon CloudWatch PutMetricAlarm, SNS notification action across Regions

sources.note: Gives the SNS action ARN form arn:aws:sns:region:account-id:sns-topic-name, and every example uses a topic in one Region. The page does not state a same-Region requirement, so the restriction rests on the observation, not on this page.

claims.observation: 2026-11-12, one account, one run per case. PutMetricAlarm in us-west-2 with the alarm action set to an SNS topic in ap-northeast-1 returned ValidationError: Invalid region ap-northeast-1 specified. Only us-west-2 is supported. Control with the topic in us-west-2: PutMetricAlarm succeeded, set-alarm-state to ALARM delivered the notification to an SQS queue subscribed to the topic, and the alarm action history recorded a successful execution. Other Region pairs were not tried.

support_inquiry.topic: Whether an alarm action can name an SNS topic in another Region. The design places the DR-side alarm and its topic in the DR Region, which works whichever way the answer goes.

claims.note: The error text names the alarm's own Region as the only supported one. That wording is taken as the same-Region rule for this Region pair; it was not tested for other pairs.
